voice: A Peter Lorre-inspired nervous fixer: soft-spoken, ingratiating, watchful, and calculating, with selective 1926 underworld slang but no phonetic gangster caricature.

entries.text: I do not handle stolen goods anymore, toots. And that is not very interesting, either.
Swell. Simply swell. First I make a sawbuck on Tunney in Philly, and now I am rubbing elbows with high society. Thank you for asking.
An ankh? Certainly. That is when you are nervous. For example: "I have a great deal of ankh about returning to the slammer." You see?
Think nothing of it.
Augustini...Augustini...the name rings a bell.
Of course. Is he not the concierge at the Plaza?
I know the dagger was lifted. I may even know who did it. Knowing and saying, however, are two very different businesses.
I have a suspicion, nothing solid. Besides, what have the police done for me lately?
I am protecting me. A neglected responsibility, I assure you. Now please go.
The new museum president? A stodgy old gentleman, but a fine man. Yes. A very fine man.
Glad you asked. Back Mudlark in the third at Belmont. The horse adores a wet track.
I know nothing about any stinking cheese.
Why would I know anything about a lady like the Countess? She would have nothing to do with me. Nothing at all. Why do you ask?
She said that? It is not true. That woman could not keep a secret if her life depended on it, and I am not taking the fall for her.
Now leave me alone before I call the police.
Or somebody.
Certainly. Crodfoller is one of the most respectable men I know. Keeps his nose clean, but knows how to enjoy himself.
Why would I know anything about that? You must have me confused with somebody else.
Do I look like a specialist in ancient bones?
Not me, lady. Some very rough customers spend their time down there.
We discussed that before. I told you the riddle Rameses passed along.
Nothing beyond what Najeer tells me. He knows the Egypt business. Did I tell you the riddle he gave me?
It was something like, "What is the room you leave without entering?" and then, "What is the room you enter without leaving?"
That is supposed to be a very clever riddle. Personally, I prefer the one about the traveling salesman and the farmer's daughter. Have you heard it?
Ernie Leach? The name does not ring a bell.
And here I thought I knew every leech in town.
If I knew who that belonged to, would I be standing here discussing it with you? No, I would not.
Heimlich? No, I do not believe I have heard of him.
Do I look like a doctor? All I know is that I keep away from them.
John Bow? Is that not what they call a stiff when nobody knows his name?
That's John Doe.
Exactly. Never heard of him.
Lanterns are outside my field of expertise.
Laundry...ah, yes, washing clothes. No, I attend to that myself.
They make a dark room less dark. That is the full extent of my expertise.
Lo Fat is not in my privileged circle of friends and acquaintances.
My eyes have never required one.
Because there is no icebox upstairs? These appetizers are hopeless, and there are some hungry fellows here. I would not wave a steak around if I were you.
Nothing in this museum is quite what it seems. The same is true of its distinguished guests. Appearances deceive. Do I look like the brother of a famous Broadway producer? No--but I am.
Some days New York is a rich melting pot; other days it is a cesspool. Either way, you rise to the top and keep your feet and your nose clean. That is how I manage.
I have no need for a notebook. I already know everything.
That woman frightens me. I have been avoiding her.
Most policemen in this town stink. O'Riley is different. He understands how to treat a useful mouthpiece, and I have made good money keeping my ears open for him.
Please, little lady, I was at the party the entire time. Do not make accusations. I did not know the man, and I had no reason to kill him. Now go away.
Certainly. The elegant fellow who brought the pigsticker from Egypt. He is around here somewhere. A rather high-hat gentleman, if you will pardon my French.
No. You are not putting that on me. I have never seen the thing before in my life.
I could obtain one for you very cheaply, if you are interested.
Very well. You cannot blame a man for asking; there is no need to bite my head off.
You might call me a freelance detective. I discover things the police cannot, then pass the information along. For a price.
They could scarcely do their jobs without me. Fine men, the police. They keep me solvent. Salt of the earth.
Reporting never interested me, though I could have been a journalist if I had chosen. I have a natural respect for confidential sources.
Rameses is a quiet fellow, most of the time. An accountant, I believe. He knows his numbers, but his riddles are murder.
I like keys. They suggest possibilities.
I have the constitution of an ox. Never needed smelling salts. They would not work anyway; my nose has been broken several times.
A snake lasso? Of course. Yee-haw, little boa constrictor.
I had an uncle who sold the stuff. I always suspected it was bunk.
You have seen the speakeasy; I saw you there. It is what it is. Listen to me--I am becoming a philosopher.
Steve? The dockworker. I know the man, though he is not in my inner circle. I cannot tell you much about him.
The newspaper? Not me, sister. I prefer my news straight from the horse's patootie, if you understand me.
Tut Smith? That must be an alias. It sounds like a pharaoh on the lam.
Do not ask me, lady. I have not touched a drop of that stuff in years.
I know nothing about Watney Little's file. Nothing at all. Please stop asking.
Never heard of the rat.
Yvette is a nice working girl. I knew her before the museum, when gentlemen paid for her company. She is respectable now, so she would rather I forgot.
Watch your mouth. You are talking to him.
I cannot help you with that, toots.
How many times will you ask me? I have already told you everything I know.
It is not mine, but I will share a trade secret: there is a way to read what was typed on carbon paper.
I will not tell you precisely how, or they will throw me out of the Stoolie's Union. But it can be done.
You should not be carrying that around. You will spoil the barbecue.
No, thank you. It sticks to the roof of my mouth.
That is the real pigsticker. Take it to the copper, girlie.
No, thank you. There is very little market for oversized bones.
Thank you, toots. Do that again.
What are you looking for--one wise guy? No? Never mind.
A lightbulb. How thrilling.
If you care to cook it for me first, I would be happy to oblige.
I am not taking anything from you, lady. For all I know, that ankh is stolen.
Keep it. Perhaps you can take notes in it.
It looks like something a jockey might use.
What is this, Eau de Snake? Keep it away from me; it stinks.
Perhaps I have. Perhaps I have not. What is the information worth to you?
Then I am afraid I have no rumors for you, toots.
No dice, lady. Find your own drink. This is an open bar; every man for himself.
No, thank you. I never examine another man's rap sheet. Professional courtesy.
Hold on to those. They could be useful. I use my snips all the time.
That diary could be valuable in the proper hands. Personal papers can be terribly incriminating. I would hold on to it if I were you, but that is all I will say.
A compact, carefully dressed man with large, nervous eyes. His smooth manner cannot quite conceal the suspicion that he expects trouble from every direction.
A cloud of expensive cologne and nervous perspiration follows Ziggy wherever he goes.
